title: Tungsten chain

chokepoint.physics: Mine + APT + carbide processing; ~80% China for decades

eyebrow: Product-chain pilot · the metal that cuts the others
h1: You can't machine metal without tungsten — and China has about 80%
deck: Tungsten carbide is the hardest common industrial material: it makes the cutting tools, drill bits and wear parts that manufacture almost everything else, and the armour-piercing penetrators that make it a defence metal. China has mined roughly 80% of the world's tungsten for decades — and in 2025 added it to its export-control list.
byline: scheelite / wolframite (~80% CN) ≠ APT ≠ tungsten carbide / metal powder ≠ cutting tools & penetrators
correction: Tungsten is a quiet, persistent chokepoint. It is not a new-technology metal — it is the material that lets industry machine and drill everything else, plus a hard, dense defence material with no easy substitute in penetrators. China has held ~80% of mining for decades and dominates the APT and carbide processing steps, and in February 2025 it placed tungsten under export controls — turning a long-standing dominance into an active lever.

history.title: A dominance that never loosened: China's tungsten share, 2000 → 2024
history.note: BGS/USGS mine production, from the atlas's own data. Unlike the metals whose concentration grew or moved, China's tungsten share has simply sat near 80% for the whole period, with Vietnam a distant second. This is a stable, structural chokepoint — which is exactly what makes its addition to the export-control list in 2025 consequential.

hops.t: scheelite and wolframite ore — China ~80%, Vietnam a distant second
ore refined to ammonium paratungstate (APT), the traded chemical intermediate
APT → tungsten oxide → metal powder → tungsten carbide
cutting tools, drill bits, wear parts; penetrators and heavy alloys

panels.text: China has mined around 80% of the world's tungsten for as long as the modern record runs, holding the bulk of reserves and the processing capacity. Where other chains show concentration being built or moving downstream, tungsten's has simply persisted — a structural dominance that Western mines (in Europe, Australia and North America) have periodically tried, and mostly failed, to dent on cost.

It is not only the mine: China dominates the conversion of ore into ammonium paratungstate (APT) and tungsten carbide powder, the forms industry actually buys. So even tungsten mined elsewhere often routes through Chinese processing — the same ore-map-versus-processing-map split seen with rare earths and graphite.

sections.h2: 2 · Why nothing else machines like it

panels.text: Tungsten carbide is second only to diamond in hardness, keeps its edge at high temperature and is extremely dense. That makes it the default for cutting tools, drill bits and dies that shape every other metal, and — in dense heavy alloys — for armour-piercing penetrators and munitions. Substitutes exist for some tools, but for high-performance machining and defence, tungsten holds, so the dependence is deep and quiet.
panels.note: ITIA; USGS: carbides are the leading use.
panels.flag: it makes the tools that make everything

panels.text: In February 2025 China added tungsten (with several other metals) to its export-control list, converting a long-standing structural dominance into an active policy instrument — the same playbook applied to gallium, germanium, graphite and rare-earth magnets. Because tungsten gates both civilian manufacturing and defence production, and recycling and Western mines cover only part of demand, the lever is a serious one.
panels.flag: the same export-control playbook (see the defence chain)

trade_intro: BACI carries tungsten ores (261100), ammonium paratungstate and other tungstates (284180) and unwrought tungsten and powder (810194), but not finished carbide tools or the tungsten in munitions.
